newsitem.title: UK: Night flight problem for Caribbean drug patrol.
newsitem.headline: Night flight problem for Caribbean drug patrol.

text.p: The fight against the drugs trade in the Caribbean is being hampered because two surveillance planes provided by Britain to its dependent territories have problems flying at night, a report published on Friday said.

"The surveillance planes have limited night flying capability -- most of the flights are therefore at times when there is less risk of drug trafficking," the report from Britain's independent National Audit Office watchdog said.
The planes were given to the British Virgin Islands and the Turks and Caicos Islands, whose isolated coastlines provide ideal opportunities for drug smugglers, three years ago.
They, along with four new police boats for the British Caribbean possessions, cost 2.2 million pounds ($3.6 million).
But the report said: "The effectiveness and utilisation of UK-funded assets by local governments could be improved. In particular, the surveillance planes have had only limited impact."
It said that in 1994 and 1995 flying time of the British Virgin Islands plane was curtailed because the local government lacked funds to pay fuel bills.
And in the Turks and Caicos Islands repair bills for the plane went unpaid, delaying further essential maintenance work.
Britain has three other Caribbean dependent territories -- Anguilla, the Cayman Islands and Montserrat.
The report says the fight against drugs is also impeded by the fact that the only one of the five territories with drug analysis facilities is the Cayman Islands.
The others "must send suspicious substances to Barbados or the Bahamas for examination, causing lengthy delays", it says.

It adds that although new legislation in the territories provides more opportunity to confiscate profits from drugs-related crime, only the British Virgin Islands and the Cayman Islands have trained full-time staff dedicated to this. ($1=.6115 Pound)
